His neighbourhood, from 1902 to 1924: the studios, the Hôtel de Blois, the cafés.
1924–1928: publishers, the hotels of rue de Tournon, the oldest table in Paris.
Grand hotels, grand restaurants, the chess café and the English bookshop.
The Mathers on rue Saint-Vincent, the Grande Loge de France, the hotel on rue Frochot.
1928–1929: the last apartment, the Préfecture, the train to Brussels.
Notre-Dame, then Oscar Wilde's tomb at Père-Lachaise.
The sites of Parisian Thelemic commemorations, through the year.

bodiniere.tx: In March 1899, the Mathers gave public performances of their “Rites of Isis” here. According to his timeline, Crowley attended one of the 1899 performances and met Susan Strong there, though the venue is not named. The setting of the Parisian Golden Dawn, which he joined shortly afterwards. The hall has disappeared.
bodiniere.stn: The hall is gone; a restaurant occupies the premises.

mathers.tx: The Mathers' villa. It has three entrances (avenue Mozart, rue Ribéra and rue de la Source), hence the impression of several addresses, and housed the Ahathoor Temple No. 7, with the Vault of the Adepts painted by Moina. Rejected by the London temple, Crowley was initiated Adeptus Minor by Mathers in Paris on 16 January 1900, under the motto Parzival. In April he returned and became their envoy against the London revolt.

stvincent.tx: Mathers wrote to Yeats from this address on 12 January 1901. At the end of 1902, having fallen out with him, Crowley came here to claim his books and luggage: Mathers returned the books, but not the trunk. The street, in the heart of old Montmartre, has barely changed.
stvincent.w: Chronology to be cross-checked with Churton.

camp.tx: Crowley lodged at No. 8 bis in this artists' street in January 1903 and wrote from here to Gerald Kelly, his Cambridge friend and future brother-in-law, who was painting in Montparnasse. This was the heart of the neighbourhood's Anglo-American circle.

manray.tx: Man Ray's studio from 1922 into the 1930s. Berenice Abbott was his assistant here from 1923 to 1926. Churton recounts Crowley's affair with Abbott and his friendship with Man Ray. No source says he posed here.
manray.stn: Private studios; the façade can be seen from the street.

colarossi.tx: The painting academy where Stephen Haweis met Mina Loy around 1902-1903: the Anglo-American artistic milieu in which Crowley moved in Montparnasse.
colarossi.stn: The academy closed in the 1930s; a restaurant on the ground floor.

blois.tx: His home base for sixteen years. He moved in on 28 April 1908 after leaving Rose, returned in 1911, stayed here during the Paris Working with Victor Neuburg, from 31 December 1913 to 12 February 1914, then in 1921 and in 1924 with Leah Hirsig. The owner, M. Bourcier, gave him credit, until their eviction on 1 May 1924.
blois.w: Street number: 49 in 1908, 50 afterwards, according to the timeline.

dome.tx: During his magical retreat of 1-13 October 1908 (John St. John), he had coffee and a brioche here on the first morning and dined here on 2 October with Mary Waska. The café, opened in 1898, is still in business.

lavenue.ad: 68, boulevard du Montparnasse (angle de la rue du Départ), Paris
lavenue.tx: A hotel-restaurant founded in 1854 opposite the old Gare de l'Ouest, frequented by Rodin and Falguière. Crowley stayed here in early June 1908, the day Vanity Fair published his story “Jeremiah in the Quartier Montparnasse”, and celebrated his 33rd birthday here on 12 October: kidneys, strawberry tart, Burgundy and a cigar. It closed in 1937.
lavenue.stn: Closed in 1937; another restaurant on the corner.

chat.tx: The artists’ restaurant to which Gerald Kelly introduces him. Somerset Maugham dines here every evening and will make him the model for Oliver Haddo, the magician of his novel The Magician (1908). Arnold Bennett describes him here too. The restaurant has disappeared.

regina.tx: On 24 March 1903, he lunches here with General Hector Macdonald, a hero of the British army targeted by a scandal in London. The next day, Macdonald takes his own life in this hotel.

paillard.tx: Back from Cairo, where he had just received The Book of the Law, he lunched here on 26 April 1904 with Arnold Bennett, accompanied by his wife Rose. The restaurant has disappeared.

gldf.tx: The headquarters and temples of the Grande Loge de France from 1903 to 1911. Crowley was received here into the Anglo-Saxon Lodge No. 343: initiated on 8 October 1904, raised to Master Mason on 17 December, registered as a “poet”. In June 1913 he announced his resignation, reproaching the lodge for tolerating co-Masonry.

wilde.tx: Jacob Epstein's monument, covered with a tarpaulin on the prefect's orders, was forcibly unveiled: according to some biographers on 4 November 1913, with students from the Latin Quarter, according to others in early August 1914. Crowley took away the bronze butterfly that hid the sphinx's genitals and later handed it to Epstein at the Café Royal in London. Every 5 November, Thelemites gather here to read Liber OZ together.

nd.tx: On 22 April 1924 he visited the cathedral with Leah Hirsig, a few days before their eviction from the Hôtel de Blois.

regence.tx: The great café of chess players, where Diderot and Philidor played. Crowley, a very strong player since Cambridge, plays here on 20 and 21 January 1924. On 11 October 1928 he is playing chess, perhaps here, while Kasimira Bass runs off with 5,000 francs. The café has disappeared.
regence.stn: A plaque recalls the café at no. 161.

odeon.tx: On 7 January 1924 he met Sylvia Beach, publisher of Ulysses, to offer her his Confessions. Her bookshop was at this address.
odeon.stn: Bookshop closed in 1941; a plaque on the building.

dauphin.tx: He stayed here in May and June 1925 with Dorothy Olsen, writing poems and many letters, the year part of the German membership recognised him as head of the O.T.O.

vuillemont.tx: The hotel on rue Boissy-d'Anglas, spelled “Vuillemont” in the timeline. He was turned out on 7 August 1926 for an unpaid bill.
vuillemont.stn: Today the Sofitel Le Faubourg hotel.

frochot.tx: His Pigalle address, at the foot of Montmartre, from 26 August 1926: the Hôtel Atlantic, called the Hotel Frochot in his 1927 letters. The actress Jane Wolfe, who had come from the Abbey of Thelema, joined him here on 12 September. This was the period of the magical operations recorded in his diary. He was still here in July 1927.

mission.tx: His lodging from July to early December 1927. His daughter Astarte visited him and he took her to the circus. In 1929, Paris-Midi would speak of a “bachelor flat” of Crowley's in Auteuil, possibly this one.

foyot.nm: Hôtel Foyot and Hôtel Royal Condé
foyot.ad: 33, rue de Tournon et 10, rue de Condé, 75006 Paris
foyot.tx: From late 1927 to May 1928 he lives in room 21 of the Hôtel Foyot, facing the Senate: Gerald Yorke comes to see him here, Kasimira Bass arrives on 5 March, and on 22 March he recovers the rights to The Diary of a Drug Fiend. He spends the summer of 1928 at the nearby Hôtel Royal Condé. The Foyot was demolished in the late 1930s.
foyot.stn: Demolished; a small square facing the Senate.

galignani.tx: The first English bookshop on the Continent, still open. On 12 October 1928 he buys the Golden Verses of Pythagoras here, two detective novels and a stamp. He comes back in February and March 1929.

chaise.tx: He dines here on 12 November 1928, then notes a kiss at 10:45 pm in his diary. Opened in 1680, it is one of the oldest restaurants in Paris, and it is still serving.

suffren.tx: His last Paris home, from 19 September 1928 to 16 April 1929. Kasimira Bass ran off on 11 October, Israel Regardie arrived on the 12th to become his secretary, and Gerald Yorke came to see him here in December. Here he received the proofs of Magick in Theory and Practice.

prefecture.tx: The foreigners’ department refuses him a residence permit, as it does Maria de Miramar and Regardie, and orders him to leave before 9 March 1929. Being ill, he obtains a reprieve; the Préfecture confirms the measure to the press.
prefecture.stn: Still the Police Prefecture, seen from outside.

garenord.tx: On 17 April 1929, watched by the Sûreté and the journalists, he takes the morning train to Brussels and announces that he will return. It is the end of his Paris years.

molay.tx: The last Grand Master of the Temple is burned here, on the former Île aux Juifs, on 18 March 1314; a plaque on the Pont-Neuf commemorates it. Every 18 March: reading of the eleventh Collect of Liber XV and laying of flowers.

levi.tx: Alphonse-Louis Constant, known as Éliphas Lévi, whose reincarnation Crowley claimed to be, lived and died here on 31 May 1875. The building was demolished: today it is one of the entrances of the Necker-Enfants malades hospital. He is buried at Ivry. Every 31 May: gathering, eleventh Collect, flowers.

temple.tx: Here stood the commandery of the Templars. On Friday 13 October 1307, the knights are arrested throughout France. Every 13 October: gathering, reading and flowers.

papus.tx: Doctor Gérard Encausse, known as Papus, a great figure of Parisian occultism, dies on 25 October 1916. Every 25 October: gathering at his tomb, eleventh Collect of Liber XV, flowers.

tl: The Mathers perform the “Rites of Isis” at the Bodinière.
Initiated Adeptus Minor by Mathers in Paris; back in April during the Golden Dawn revolt.
Montparnasse with Gerald Kelly, the Chat Blanc, Rodin, the falling-out with Mathers, the lunch with General Macdonald.
Back from Cairo; raised Master Mason in the Anglo-Saxon Lodge no. 343.
Hôtel de Blois. Great Magical Retirement, 1–13 October.
Hôtel de Blois from May to August; in November he leaves Paris for Switzerland with Mary d'Este Sturges.
4 November: he unveils Oscar Wilde’s tomb at Père-Lachaise.
Paris Working with Victor Neuburg, 31 December to 12 February: 24 operations.
Two months at the Hôtel de Blois, away from the Abbey of Thelema; he initiates Mary Butts.
January to May at the Hôtel de Blois with Leah Hirsig.
Hôtel du Dauphin with Dorothy Olsen.
Pigalle, Auteuil, then rue de Tournon: his longest Paris years.
Residence refused; departure from the Gare du Nord for Brussels on 17 April.

h: At 18 rue Saint-Lazare, in the 9th arrondissement, Charles Bodinier (1844-1911), former secretary general of the Comédie-Française who had run the Théâtre d'Application since 1888, opened a small hall in 1890 that soon became known as La Bodinière. It lived mainly on “matinées-causeries”: afternoon lectures, often followed by recitals, before an audience of aristocrats, wealthy bourgeois and intellectuals. Anatole France, François Coppée, Maurice Donnay and Francisque Sarcey spoke there; Robert de Montesquiou gave a lecture there on 17 January 1894 with the participation of Sarah Bernhardt, and Yvette Guilbert sang there in 1891 between two talks by Hugues Le Roux. Shadow-theatre shows were also staged there.

The venue was no stranger to esoteric circles. In March 1892, Paul Fort's Théâtre d'Art presented its last programme there, which included Les Noces de Sathan by Jules Bois, a writer close to MacGregor Mathers; the evening was a failure. Seven years later, in March 1899 according to the entry on Moina Mathers, the Mathers couple performed their “Rites of Isis” there in public, Egyptianising ceremonies they had until then celebrated in private settings: MacGregor played the hierophant Rameses, Moina the high priestess Anari. These performances helped make the Parisian Golden Dawn known beyond the circle of initiates.

Crowley's presence in the hall is not directly documented. The Aleister Crowley Timeline, however, places his first meeting with Mathers in Paris around May 1899 and states that he then attended the original stage production of the Rites of Isis, where he met the singer Susan Strong; the source does not name the theatre, and the date differs from the March date given elsewhere. Crowley, initiated into the Golden Dawn in London in November 1898, then rose rapidly through the order's first grades during 1899, before being received by Mathers in Paris in January 1900.
La Bodinière closed in 1902. According to Wikipedia, the premises at 18 rue Saint-Lazare are now occupied by a restaurant; the sources report no visible trace of the former lecture hall.

Settled in Paris from 1892 (MacGregor Mathers arrived on 21 May), the Mathers moved several times for lack of money. Their most lasting home, near the Bois de Boulogne, was a villa in the Auteuil district with three entrances and therefore three addresses: 87 avenue Mozart, 43 rue Ribéra and 14 rue de la Source. It was there, according to historians of the order, that the Golden Dawn's Ahathoor Temple No. 7 operated, consecrated on 6 January 1894 in the presence of Annie Horniman; Moina, who taught there, decorated its walls with figures of Egyptian gods painted in oils. Papus (Gérard Encausse) was a member, and W. B. Yeats visited the Mathers in Paris several times between 1897 and 1899 to work with them on Celtic rituals.

Crowley, who had joined the Golden Dawn in London in 1898, was refused entry to the Second Order by the London adepts. He took the night boat to Paris on 15 January 1900 and, the next day, Tuesday 16 January, Mathers initiated him into the grade of Adeptus Minor under the motto Parzival. The London adepts refused to recognise this reception; one history of the order also notes that it does not appear in the records of the Ahathoor Temple, which further fuels the debate.

Crowley returned on 8 April 1900. On the 9th he discussed the revolt of the London temple with MacGregor and Moina and became their representative; on the 12th Mathers gave him instructions and symbols, and he left again on the 13th at 11:50 a.m. On 17 April he tried to take over the Second Order's premises at 36 Blythe Road in London, but the attempt came to nothing and the lawsuit was lost on 28 April. The timeline places these meetings “in Paris” without giving the address; that they took place at the Auteuil villa is therefore likely but not established by the sources.

Towards the end of 1900, the Mathers left Auteuil for Montmartre. The sources do not say what remains of the villa: avenue Mozart, rue Ribéra and rue de la Source now enclose a residential block in the 16th arrondissement, where one can only spot the three street numbers from the street.

h: Rue Saint-Vincent winds along the northern slope of the Butte Montmartre, behind the Sacré-Cœur. At the turn of the century it was still an almost rural corner: at the junction with rue des Saules, the Lapin Agile cabaret, named after its sign painted by André Gill, drew painters and poets, while a high wall hid the small Saint-Vincent cemetery, where Utrillo, Marcel Aymé and Marcel Carné would later be buried. The Clos Montmartre vineyard, on the other hand, came later: it was replanted in the 1930s by the Société du Vieux Montmartre to save the land from property development.

The Mathers settled in Montmartre towards the end of 1900. In December of that year the journalist André Gaucher published an article titled “Isis à Montmartre” in L'Écho du Merveilleux: he described an Isiac ceremony to which he had been invited in the couple's new home, where the crates had not yet been unpacked but which offered a larger temple and a garden. On 12 January 1901, MacGregor Mathers dated from 28 rue Saint-Vincent a furious letter to W. B. Yeats, whom he accused of siding with the London “rebels”; in it he also denounced the Horoses, a pair of adventurers who had borrowed rituals and books from him without returning them.

Crowley, who had left at the end of 1900 for Mexico and then Asia, returned via Egypt in the autumn of 1902. On 25 October he wrote from Cairo to Gerald Kelly that he would reach Paris via Marseille and suggested a reunion dinner to which the Mathers might be invited. According to Tobias Churton (Aleister Crowley in Paris), relations then soured: Mathers was reserved and some of Crowley's luggage could not be found. The more detailed account of a visit to rue Saint-Vincent in November 1902, with books returned but a trunk withheld, has yet to be checked against Churton's book.

Today rue Saint-Vincent remains one of the quietest streets on the Butte, lined with gardens, the vineyard and the cemetery, with the Lapin Agile still in business. The sources do not describe the building at No. 28.

South of boulevard du Montparnasse, rue Campagne-Première became at the turn of the 20th century one of the densest artists' streets in Paris, just as painters and writers were leaving Montmartre for Montparnasse. Eugène Atget had his studio at No. 17 from 1898 to 1927; the cité at No. 9 was built with materials salvaged from the 1889 Exposition Universelle; the Hôtel Istria, at No. 29, would later host Satie, Duchamp, Picabia, Tzara and Kiki. Modigliani, Foujita, Kandinsky, Rilke and many others passed through.

Crowley arrived in Paris via Marseille in the autumn of 1902, returning from the K2 expedition and a stay in Egypt. As early as October he told Gerald Kelly, his Cambridge friend who had become a painter in Paris, that he would lodge in Montparnasse rather than in Kelly's street, and that he wished to keep a low profile. A letter to Kelly bears the address 8 bis rue Campagne-Première and the date, in square brackets, Wednesday 14 January 1903: in it Crowley offers his condolences to his friend, struck by bad family news. Kelly then had a studio in Montparnasse, but the sources do not specify that it was in this street.

These months of 1902-1903 were when Crowley moved in Rodin's circle, to whom he devoted the poems “Rodin” and “Balzac”, translated into French by Marcel Schwob; Rodin wrote to him on 25 February and 14 March 1903. It was also through Kelly that he met Stephen Haweis, and Kelly who introduced him to his sister Rose, who had joined him in Paris in 1902 and whom Crowley would marry on 12 August 1903. In February he left Paris for the Côte d'Azur.

The street has kept many of its studios, now rare in Paris, as well as several remarkable façades, including the ceramic-clad building at No. 31. The sources say nothing about the building at No. 8 bis itself.

h: No. 31-31 bis rue Campagne-Première is a building of studios and apartments built by the architect André Arfvidson on a plot bought in 1901 by Charles-Henry Bréal; begun in 1911, it won a prize in the City of Paris façade competition. Its façade is clad in flambé stoneware by the ceramicist Alexandre Bigot, and its large glass windows light duplex studios that herald modern architecture. It has been listed as a historic monument since 12 June 1986. Chaïm Soutine, Dora Maar, César and Pierre Restany lived or worked there.

Having arrived in Paris in July 1921, Man Ray left his room at the Hôtel des Écoles, rue Delambre, in 1922 for a ground-floor duplex studio at No. 31 bis, which he occupied for about fourteen years. The lower level was used for visits, collages and objects, a mezzanine served as a bedroom, and two small rooms became darkrooms. Kiki de Montparnasse was then his companion. The American Berenice Abbott was his assistant there from 1923 to 1925 or 1926, depending on the source: she first learned printing, then photography, before opening her own studio. It was also through Man Ray that she discovered the work of Eugène Atget, a neighbour at No. 17.

Crowley lived mainly in Paris from 1924 to 1929. Tobias Churton, in Aleister Crowley in Paris, describes his affair with Berenice Abbott and his friendship with Man Ray. The Aleister Crowley Timeline mentions Abbott under the date 10 November 1926, for a sex-magick operation with Crowley; by that date she had already left Man Ray's studio to work on her own account. No source indicates that Crowley posed or stayed at No. 31 bis: the link with this place runs through the two photographers.

The building is easy to see from the street: its flambé stoneware façade and large glass windows are one of the sights of the neighbourhood. The studios remain private homes and are not open to visitors.

h: The Académie Colarossi descended from the Académie Suisse, a free studio founded around 1815 on the quai des Orfèvres, on the Île de la Cité. Taken over by the Italian model and sculptor Filippo Colarossi, it moved to 10 rue de la Grande-Chaumière in the 1870s (1879 according to Wikipedia). Unlike the École des Beaux-Arts, it admitted women and allowed them to draw from the nude model, male models included. Raphaël Collin, Gustave Courtois and the sculptor Injalbert taught there; Alphonse Mucha gave a course there in 1900. Camille Claudel, Jeanne Hébuterne, Modigliani and Emily Carr were among its students. The street was also home to the Chez Charlotte crèmerie and, from 1904, the Académie de la Grande Chaumière.

The academy was a fixture of the Anglo-American milieu of Montparnasse that Crowley frequented in 1902-1903. The English painter and photographer Stephen Haweis studied there after the death of his parents, and it was there that he met the young Mina Loy, in 1902 according to one account, in 1903 according to the poet's chronology; they married on 31 December 1903. Haweis later became the photographer of a large part of Rodin's work. According to the description of Tobias Churton's book, it was Gerald Kelly who introduced Haweis to Crowley, at a time when Crowley was moving in Rodin's circle.

Nothing indicates that Crowley himself took classes at Colarossi. As for Moina Mathers, the sources mention her training at the Slade School in London (1883-1886), but not the Académie Colarossi: this point remains to be verified.

The academy closed in the 1930s. At No. 10 a restaurant now occupies the ground floor, while the nearby Académie de la Grande Chaumière still welcomes drawing students; the street retains the atmosphere of a small street of studios near the carrefour Vavin.

h: The Hôtel de Blois was a modest furnished hotel on rue Vavin, a stone's throw from the crossroads of the same name and the cafés of Montparnasse, in a street that also acquired, in 1912-1914, the stepped building by Henri Sauvage and Charles Sarazin at No. 26. Its owner, M. Bourcier, often let Crowley stay on credit. The address varies between sources: the Aleister Crowley Timeline gives 49 rue Vavin for 1908, then 50 for all subsequent years.

Crowley moved in on 28 April 1908, after leaving Rose Kelly, and spent the summer working there on several texts before setting off on 31 July with Victor Neuburg on a walking tour of Spain. He returned in 1911 (from 30 April to 3 May, then in August) and stayed there on 30 January 1914, during the “Paris Working”. This series of sex-magick operations carried out with Neuburg began on the night of 31 December 1913 with an invocation of Mercury (Thoth) and ended on 12 February 1914 with the twenty-fourth; Jupiter was the other principal deity, and Walter Duranty took part. The published text does not specify where the sessions were held, some of which took place at the homes of friends such as Jane Chéron: the hotel is therefore the likely, though not certain, setting for the whole.

Back from Cefalù, Crowley stayed there from late January to 31 March 1921; there he initiated the writer Mary Butts into the first degree of the O.T.O. on 11 March. In 1924 he lived there from 15 January to 1 May, ill and penniless: on 8 March he pawned everything to send Norman Mudd to London, received Nina Hamnett, and Leah Hirsig joined him there on 29 March. On 1 May both were turned out for unpaid rent and left for 6 rue Jolia.
The sources do not say what became of the Hôtel de Blois. A hotel, the Hôtel Atelier Vavin, exists today at 49 rue Vavin, but no document establishes that it is the same establishment.

Le Dôme opened in 1898 at the corner of boulevard du Montparnasse and rue Delambre. Its founder, Paul Chambon, from the Auvergne, first ran it as a small neighbourhood bar-tabac. From around 1905, Scandinavian, German and American artists made it their headquarters, to the point that it was nicknamed the Anglo-American café; before 1914 it was considered the smartest café in Montparnasse, while still allowing a penniless artist to eat there for next to nothing. Its regulars, the “Dômiers”, would form an illustrious list: Picasso, Kandinsky, Pascin, Soutine, Man Ray, Hemingway, Ezra Pound, Walter Benjamin and Samuel Beckett.

Crowley himself was one of the Dômiers. On 1 October 1908 he began in Paris a magical retreat of about ten days, whose diary would be published under the title John St. John: he wanted to test whether a precise spiritual result, communion with his Holy Guardian Angel, could be attained without leaving city life, by disciplining his thoughts and cutting down on food and sleep. On the first morning, after buying the notebook intended for this diary, he went to the Dôme for coffee and a brioche and wrote the opening of his account there; he returned in the afternoon for a citron pressé. In the evening, Nina Olivier introduced him to Mary Waska, with whom he dined and spent the night. According to the timeline, he dined with her again at the Dôme on 2 October.

The retreat continued until 13 October. During it Crowley illuminated Liber Pyramidos from the 5th and sat from the 7th to the 12th for the sculptor Michael Brenner. The diary also mentions oysters and a beefsteak ordered at noon on the first day, without naming the restaurant.

Le Dôme still exists at 108 boulevard du Montparnasse. Now an upmarket seafood restaurant, once awarded a Michelin star, it retains an Art Deco interior of wood panelling and stained glass, a few steps from the carrefour Vavin.

h: The Maison Lavenue, also known as the Hôtel de France et de Bretagne, stood at the corner of boulevard du Montparnasse (No. 68) and rue du Départ (Nos. 1-3), facing place de Rennes, now place du 18-Juin-1940. It was a stone's throw from the old Gare de l'Ouest, whose departure platforms rue du Départ had run alongside since 1849. The façade bears the dates 1854 and 1897: the first corresponds to its foundation, the second to the renovation carried out by M. Gruffaz, who had taken over the business after the sudden death of his predecessor, M. Charuet, in 1890.

The hotel-restaurant was popular with artists. In The Real Latin Quarter (1901), Frank Berkeley Smith lists among its regulars Auguste Rodin, Alexandre Falguière, Jean-Paul Laurens, Léon Bonnat, Whistler, Sargent and the American sculptors Saint-Gaudens and MacMonnies. The house also hosted political dinners, notably those of the Patrie française, with Maurice Barrès and François Coppée. It went bankrupt in 1937.

Crowley moved in at the beginning of June 1908. The Aleister Crowley Timeline places him on 3 June at the “Hotel Lavenue, place de Rennes”, the very day the London Vanity Fair published his story “Jeremiah in the Quartier Montparnasse”, soon followed by “Ezekiel in the Quartier Montparnasse” (22 August). He had left his wife Rose Kelly at the end of April and that summer also stayed at the Hôtel de Blois, rue Vavin. In the autumn he returned to Paris for a major magical retreat begun on 1 October and completed on the 13th; the diary he kept of it would be published under the title John St. John.

It was during this retreat that he had a birthday lunch at Lavenue's, recorded at 12:40 p.m. in his diary according to the Culinary Crowley website: well-cooked kidneys, strawberry tart, a Burgundy he praised lavishly, coffee, cognac and a Cuban cigar he judged the best of his life. Crowley was born on 12 October 1875; the same article, however, places the eve of his birthday on the evening of the 12th, which would suggest the 13th, so the exact date of the meal needs to be checked against the text of John St. John.

After the bankruptcy, the corner housed the Chez Dupont restaurant and the Miramar cinema, later taken over by Gaumont, then a Taverne de Maître Kanter until 1994; a grill-restaurant chain occupies it today, and the corner pharmacy has survived through the eras. From the street, the dates 1854 and 1897 can still be read on the façade, the only visible reminder of the house.

Le Chat Blanc was a small restaurant on rue d'Odessa, close to the Gare Montparnasse, where a circle of English-speaking artists and writers dined in the early 20th century. According to Somerset Maugham's recollections, the same diners met there almost every evening and gave passing visitors a rather cool welcome. Maugham met Arnold Bennett and the critic Clive Bell there. Samuel J. Rogal, author of an encyclopedia devoted to Maugham, sees it as the model for the restaurant the novelist calls “Gravier's” in Of Human Bondage (1915).

It was the painter Gerald Kelly, Crowley's future brother-in-law, who took Maugham there, and Maugham got into the habit of dining there every evening. Crowley, back in Paris at the end of 1902 and lodging at 8 bis rue Campagne-Première in early 1903, was among the occasional visitors. Maugham describes him as a brilliant, boastful and amusing talker, whom he found unlikeable but interesting, and who talked to him about magic and occultism. Rogal dates their meeting to 1904.

Bennett, for his part, recorded in his journal on 9 March 1905 a dinner at the Chat Blanc in Crowley's presence, noting his dirty hands, his large rings, hair that seemed to him dyed, a showy waistcoat, a fur coat and tennis shoes.

Maugham wrote The Magician in the first half of 1907; the novel appeared in 1908. In it he gave his magus, Oliver Haddo, many of Crowley's traits, while making him more sinister and attributing real powers to him. Crowley recognised himself and responded with a long review published in Vanity Fair on 30 December 1908, signed “Oliver Haddo”; Maugham claims never to have read it.

The restaurant has disappeared and the sources report no plaque. Rue d'Odessa still exists, in the shadow of the Tour Montparnasse; No. 13 is identified by a photographer as the former site of the Chat Blanc.

h: The Hôtel Regina was born of the initiative of Léonard Tauber and Constant Baverez, who decided in 1898 to turn a building on place des Pyramides into a luxury hotel. The works, entrusted to the architect Armand Sibien, lasted about two years, and the establishment opened for the 1900 Exposition Universelle. Its name, a tribute to Queen Victoria, was meant to salute the Franco-British rapprochement. Facing its windows stands Emmanuel Frémiet's gilded equestrian Joan of Arc, unveiled in 1874. In 1919, representatives of the Allied Red Cross societies met there, a meeting that led to the future international federation.

On 24 March 1903, Crowley, then living in Montparnasse, lunched there with Major General Sir Hector Macdonald, who had recognised him in the restaurant's dining room, according to the Aleister Crowley Timeline. The son of Highland crofters, who had enlisted as a private in the Gordon Highlanders, Macdonald had covered himself in glory at Omdurman in 1898 and had commanded the British troops in Ceylon since 1902.

Rumours about his relations with young boys had driven him to return to Europe. In London, Lord Roberts had advised him to go back and face a court martial. The day after the lunch, 25 March 1903, he discovered in a morning newspaper, at the Regina, that the accusations had been made public, went back up to his room and took his own life. A commission concluded in June that no evidence supported the accusations. Some thirty thousand people attended his funeral in Edinburgh. The novelist Jake Arnott drew on this encounter for his novel The Devil's Paintbrush.

Crowley returned to the Regina the following year: the timeline places him there on 16 and 18 October 1904, a few days after his Masonic initiation, when he visited the Salon d'Automne at the Grand Palais.

The hotel still exists, run by the descendants of Constant Baverez, and was renovated between 2013 and 2015. From place des Pyramides one can see the Art Nouveau stone façade and a plaque recalling the former royal riding school that occupied the site.

h: The Paillard restaurant stood at the corner of rue de la Chaussée-d'Antin and boulevard des Italiens, at No. 2 of the street. The collections of the Bibliothèque historique de la Ville de Paris present it as the continuation of the Maison Maire, and the chef Léopold Mourier, who joined Maire in 1883, became its head chef in 1886, at a time when the house belonged to a Madame Paillard. The website devoted to the painter Guirand de Scévola dates the establishment to 1878 and describes it as a meeting place for the Tout-Paris and crowned heads during the Belle Époque. An annex, the “Petit Paillard”, was located on the Champs-Élysées.

In 1905, Guirand de Scévola decorated the ceiling of the main dining room with a composition titled La Femme au vingtième siècle, unveiled in early October; the press thought it recognised Cléo de Mérode, La Belle Otero or Polaire in it. No photograph of this ceiling has been found.

On Tuesday 26 April 1904, Crowley and his wife Rose Kelly, sister of the painter Gerald Kelly, invited Arnold Bennett by telegram to lunch at Paillard. The couple were returning from Egypt: a few weeks earlier, in Cairo, Crowley had received Liber AL vel Legis, or The Book of the Law, and he left Paris the very next day for London and then Boleskine. Bennett noted in his journal a red waistcoat studded with jewels and the largest ring he had ever seen; he added that he found Crowley rather likeable. The conversation turned to how a great brain works, then to Oscar Wilde, Crowley claiming to know a man who had supposedly met him in the Pyrenees while he was in prison.

In Egypt, Crowley had presented himself under the name “Prince Chioa Khan”; the timeline mentions him in February 1904 at Helwan. Bennett's journal does not say that he was still using this name in Paris, but his attire shows that he was still cultivating this Oriental persona.

The 19th-century establishment has disappeared. A photograph by André Gandner, held at the Musée de la Libération de Paris, still shows an “Au Paillard” sign at this corner in 1944, with the Église de la Trinité at the end of the street. An online directory listed a chain restaurant of that name at No. 2 in 2015; the corner building can be seen from the crossroads, but the sources mention no surviving original decoration.

h: The Grande Loge de France, formed in 1894 from the unification of the lodges of the Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite, received full administration of the first three degrees from the Supreme Council in 1904. It had about 3,000 members at its founding and 8,400 in 1912. From 1903 its headquarters and temples were at 42 rue Rochechouart, in the 9th arrondissement. The premises soon became too cramped, and in July 1911 the obedience bought a former Franciscan convent to move into.

Among its lodges was the Anglo-Saxon Lodge No. 343, constituted in 1899 by the Grande Loge de France; according to Crowley, initiations there followed the English ritual. Wikipedia lists it among the lodges of the period devoted to the study of symbolism. It was not recognised by the United Grand Lodge of England; it later joined the Grande Loge nationale française.

On 29 June 1904, Crowley submitted his application for membership there under the name Aleister St. Edward Crowley, profession “poet”; the petition was countersigned by the secretary, the Reverend James Lyon Bowley, and by the Worshipful Master Edward-Philip Denny. He was initiated on 8 October 1904 and raised to Master Mason on 17 December of the same year. These were the months following the reception of The Book of the Law in Cairo that spring.

In 1913, Crowley sought to have his Masonic standing recognised in England. In a letter of 27 June to Sir Edward Letchworth, Grand Secretary at Freemasons' Hall, he recalled his raising in Lodge 343 and announced that he saw no other course than to resign, having learned that the Grande Loge de France tolerated, or even recognised, co-Masonry, which he attacked violently. Only a draft of this correspondence survives, and the English reply is not known.

The rue Rochechouart headquarters was occupied only from 1903 to 1911. The sources describe neither the later history of the building nor any traces of its Masonic past; from the street one sees only an ordinary façade of the neighbourhood, with no plaque reported.

h: Oscar Wilde, who died on 30 November 1900 at the Hôtel d'Alsace, was first buried in the Parisian cemetery of Bagneux. In 1909 his literary executor Robert Ross acquired a plot in the 89th division of Père-Lachaise and had his remains transferred there. The monument, funded by Helen Carew, was entrusted to Jacob Epstein: a large winged sphinx carved from a block of Hopton Wood stone weighing some twenty tonnes, on a base designed by Charles Holden, shown to the London press in June 1912 and then installed in Paris in September.

The figure's nudity caused outrage. Customs demanded a duty of 120 pounds, the Préfecture de la Seine had the monument covered with a tarpaulin and placed under the guard of a gendarme, and the genitals were even plastered over. The sphinx remained hidden for nearly two years; Epstein and his friends removed the tarpaulin several times, only for it to be immediately put back. To break the deadlock, Ross had a bronze plaque in the shape of a butterfly fitted, a solution the sculptor strongly disliked.

Crowley's role is known from several accounts that disagree on the date. The version adopted by Wikipedia and by Ellen Crowell's study places in August 1914 an unveiling presided over by Crowley, which Epstein refused to attend; a few weeks later, Crowley is said to have met the sculptor wearing the bronze butterfly as a pendant, and to have handed it to Epstein one evening at the Café Royal in London. Another tradition, reported elsewhere, speaks of a forcible unveiling on 4 November 1913 with students from the Latin Quarter; it could not be confirmed. Crowley's timeline, which places him in Switzerland and then in London in early August 1914, also calls for caution regarding the latter date.

The monument has continued to attract acts of devotion and vandalism: in 1961 the sphinx's genitals were broken off and have never been found; Ross's ashes were placed in the tomb in 1950. As lipstick kisses had damaged the stone, the tomb was cleaned in 2011 and surrounded by a glass barrier about two metres high.
Listed as a historic monument on 10 March 1995, the tomb can be visited freely in the 89th division. One can see Epstein's sphinx behind its glass and the inscription carved by Joseph Cribb.

Notre-Dame Cathedral, built on the Île de la Cité from the 12th century onwards, has come down through the centuries as one of the great Gothic sanctuaries of Europe. Restored to worship in 1802 after the Revolution, it hosted on 2 December 1804 the coronation of Napoleon, who crowned himself in the presence of Pope Pius VII before crowning Joséphine. Victor Hugo's novel, published in 1831, drew public attention to the state of the building; the restoration, decided in 1843 and begun in 1845 under the direction of Lassus and Viollet-le-Duc, then of the latter alone after 1857, restored the sculptures, the gargoyles and the spire torn down in 1792.

In April 1924, Crowley was going through a difficult period. Having arrived from Nice on 5 January, he was lodging at the Hôtel de Blois, rue Vavin, often ill, penniless, forced in March to pawn his belongings to send his disciple Norman Mudd to London. Leah Hirsig, his companion and assistant at the Abbey of Thelema in Cefalù, joined him on the morning of 29 March. On 8 April he noted the twentieth anniversary of the dictation of the first chapter of The Book of the Law.

It is in this context that the Aleister Crowley Timeline records, on 22 April 1924, a visit to Notre-Dame with Leah Hirsig, with no further detail on what they did there. A week later, on 1 May, the couple were evicted from the Hôtel de Blois for unpaid rent; that same day Crowley wrote “The Blackguard and the Sage”, and Leah is recorded at 6 rue Jolia from 3 May.

The cathedral was severely damaged by the fire of 15 April 2019, which brought down Viollet-le-Duc's spire. After five years of work involving some 250 companies, it solemnly reopened on 7 December 2024 and has welcomed worshippers and visitors again since the following day. From the parvis, one can see the west front and its sculpted portals.

The Café de la Régence was born in the late 17th or early 18th century on the place du Palais-Royal: the sources hesitate between 1670, 1681 and 1718, the date adopted by the plaque installed in 2023. In the 18th century it became the great meeting place of chess players. Kermur de Légal reigned there before being dethroned by François-André Danican Philidor, a musician and reputedly the best player of his time. Diderot, who met Rousseau there in 1742, judged around 1760 that Paris was the world capital of the game and the Régence its finest venue; he noted that chessboards were rented there by the hour, at a higher price in the evening because of the candles.

Driven out by building works at the Palais-Royal, the café moved briefly to rue de Richelieu, then settled around 1854-1855 at 161 rue Saint-Honoré. The 1867 international chess tournament was played there. In the 20th century the history becomes confused: according to Wikipedia, the establishment became a restaurant in 1910, the chess room closed in 1916 and the players migrated to the Café de l'Univers, while the official plaque indicates a presence at this address until 1955.

A first-rank player since his Cambridge years, when, according to Maugham, he had represented the university, Crowley came to the Régence as soon as he arrived in Paris in January 1924. Lodging at the Hôtel de Blois, rue Vavin, he dined on 20 January with Aimée Gouraud and then went to play at the Régence, returning the next day; two days later, Norman Mudd arrived from Tunis to assist him.

On 11 October 1928, while living at 55 avenue de Suffren, Crowley left his companion Kasimira Bass in the care of Carl de Vidal Hunt while he went to a chess club that the timeline does not name. That evening she left the apartment with her clothes and 5,000 francs. The next day, the day Israel Regardie arrived, Crowley filed a complaint, then found the money under a statue; Kasimira returned on 23 October.
The café has disappeared. A plaque unveiled on 4 April 2023 at 161 rue Saint-Honoré, at the corner of avenue de l'Opéra, recalls its history and its regulars, from Philidor to Bonaparte and Musset.

Rue de l'Odéon was laid out from 1780, following the letters patent of 1779 that created the Théâtre-Français of the faubourg Saint-Germain, today's Odéon-Théâtre de l'Europe; it was first called rue du Théâtre-Français. Camille Desmoulins lived there until his arrest in 1794. It was home to Thomas Paine at No. 10 between 1797 and 1802 and, from 1915, to Adrienne Monnier's bookshop, La Maison des amis des livres, at No. 7.

Directly opposite, at No. 12, the American Sylvia Beach (1887-1962) moved Shakespeare and Company, the English-language bookshop and lending library she had opened on 19 November 1919 on rue Dupuytren. The date of the move varies between sources: 1921 in the Wikipedia article on the bookshop, 1922 in the one on the street. Hemingway, Pound, Stein and Fitzgerald frequented the shop, which Joyce used as his office; it was under this imprint that Ulysses appeared in 1922. The composer George Antheil lodged upstairs.

Crowley arrived in Paris from Nice on 5 January 1924 and saw Sylvia Beach as early as the 7th to talk to her about publishing his Confessions. The next day, alongside the entry for a day he considered particularly auspicious, his diary contains a draft of the terms he intended to propose: the matter to be kept secret, use of the shop's customer list to distribute numbered prospectuses, a 5% commission for the bookseller on each paid subscription form, and no other responsibility for her. Nothing indicates that she accepted. A few days later he settled at the Hôtel de Blois, rue Vavin, where Norman Mudd joined him from Tunis on 22 January.

In her memoirs published in 1956, Sylvia Beach recalls a brief and unpleasant encounter, without dating or locating it precisely: a blonde companion of Crowley's is said to have presented her with a prospectus and a contract already drawn up and awaiting only her signature, which alarmed her. The proportions she cites differ from those noted by Crowley. The exact location of the 7 January meeting is therefore not established, although the bookshop, where she received authors in search of a publisher every day, is the most likely setting.

Shakespeare and Company closed in December 1941, under the Occupation; Sylvia Beach was interned for six months and never reopened the shop. From the street, one now sees the building at No. 12, marked by a commemorative plaque, opposite Adrienne Monnier's former address.

h: Rue Saint-Roch, in the 1st arrondissement, links rue de Rivoli to avenue de l'Opéra, crossing rue Saint-Honoré, and runs alongside the Église Saint-Roch, whose foundation stone Louis XIV laid in 1653 and from whose steps Bonaparte had his troops fire on the royalists in October 1795. According to the Archives nationales reference database, part of the street, opened in the 16th century, was called rue du Dauphin for most of the 18th and 19th centuries, before taking in 1879 the name of the adjacent rue Saint-Roch. The name of the Hôtel du Dauphin very likely perpetuated this former name.

Crowley left Tunis on 2 May 1925 with Dorothy Olsen, his companion since the previous summer and his new “Scarlet Woman”, and William Barron, leaving Leah Hirsig behind. After a stop in Marseille, he was settled by mid-May at the Hôtel du Dauphin, 12 rue Saint-Roch, an address that appears on his correspondence until the end of June.

Many letters were sent from there: to William Bradley on several occasions, to Karl Germer on 25 May, to Heinrich Tränker, to Charles Stansfeld Jones on 14 June. Dorothy Olsen also wrote, notably to Norman Mudd. In June Crowley composed several poems intended for his Book of Oaths, including The Insensitive, Dreaming True and The Turn of the Year.

These Parisian weeks prepared a turning point. After the death of Theodor Reuss, Crowley considered himself his successor at the head of the O.T.O., and Tränker wanted to settle the question. On 21 June Crowley met Karl Germer for the first time at his home in Weida, Thuringia, then on 27 June the so-called Weida Conference was held at Tränker's home in Hohenleuben, with Germer, Hirsig, Mudd, Olsen and several German members, including Albin Grau and Eugen Grosche. Some of them recognised him, but the timeline specifies that this claim was not unanimously accepted. Crowley then remained in Thuringia all summer.

The Hôtel du Dauphin is not documented in heritage sources, and it is not known what the building at No. 12 houses today. About 390 metres long, the street still runs alongside the Église Saint-Roch, which can be seen from the pavement as Crowley saw it in 1925.

Rue Boissy-d'Anglas, in the Madeleine district, already appears on a plan of 1652; it has borne several names, including rue de la Madeleine and, for its section near the Concorde, rue des Champs-Élysées, before receiving in 1865 that of François-Antoine Boissy d'Anglas, president of the National Convention. It links place de la Concorde to boulevard Malesherbes, crossing rue du Faubourg-Saint-Honoré.

The Hôtel de Vouillemont, as spelled by the establishment that succeeded it, was an elegant address in this neighbourhood. Proust mentions it in Swann in Love, and its fashionable and foreign clientele was large; in the 1930s, Pirandello, Cocteau, Picabia and Surrealists frequented it. The same building later housed the offices of Marie Claire magazine.

Crowley stayed there at the beginning of August 1926, back from Tunisia, where he was still living at La Marsa in June. It was a difficult summer: Dorothy Olsen and Jane Wolfe had left Tunis in early July for the region of Pau, where Olsen was being treated for her gall bladder. On 6 August his address is recorded at the Hôtel Vuillemont; the next day, 7 August 1926, he was evicted for failing to pay his bill. The episode says much about the precariousness of his finances. He then went to join the two women, whom he met up with on 12 August, before returning to Paris: on 23 August he was at the Hôtel du Béarn, rue de Lille, then on the 26th he moved to rue Frochot, after a stay at a Hôtel des Ambassadeurs.

Since 2000, No. 15 of the street has been occupied by the Sofitel Paris Le Faubourg hotel, which combines two former hôtels particuliers of the 18th and 19th centuries and claims the heritage of the Hôtel de Vouillemont. The timeline devoted to Crowley, however, gives only the name of the hotel, without a number, and the sources do not specify which of the two buildings corresponded exactly to the former establishment. From the street, one sees the façades of the present hotel, a stone's throw from the Faubourg-Saint-Honoré.

h: Rue Frochot runs down to place Pigalle, where it meets avenue Frochot and rues Jean-Baptiste-Pigalle and Duperré. Both bear the name of Nicolas Frochot (1761-1828), first prefect of the Seine. The neighbouring avenue, opened in 1826, belonged to a residential development that attracted artists and art lovers; a neo-Gothic house of 1837-1839, listed as a historic monument in 2021, can still be seen there. Since the late 19th century the neighbourhood has been that of cabarets, from the Chat Noir to the Moulin Rouge, and between the wars that of bars, gambling and jazz, with an underworld reputation.

Crowley moved on 26 August 1926 into the Hôtel Atlantic, 12 rue Frochot, leaving the Hôtel des Ambassadeurs. That same day began a series of sex-magick operations recorded in his diary, which continued throughout the autumn with several partners, each operation being dedicated to a specific aim: obtaining money, youth, energy or health.

On 12 September the actress Jane Wolfe, a disciple who had come from the Abbey of Thelema in Cefalù, took a room in the same hotel. On 8 October Dorothy Olsen paid him a last visit; she left him on the 12th, his 51st birthday, went back to America and never saw him again. On 18 November he celebrated the anniversary of his entry into the Golden Dawn in 1898. The timeline also places in November 1926 an operation with the photographer Berenice Abbott.

The address remained his at least until early July 1927: on 2 July he wrote to the publisher Edward Titus from the “Hotel Frochot, 12 rue Frochot”. In the meantime, Jane Wolfe had undergone surgery at the end of April at the American Hospital in Neuilly, where she remained for eleven weeks; she sailed for New York on 1 October 1927. By mid-July, Crowley had moved to rue de la Mission-Marchand.

The sources document neither the history of the Hôtel Atlantic nor the current use of No. 12. From the street, which opens onto place Pigalle, one can see the façade of No. 12 and, close by, the entrance to avenue Frochot and its former artists' development.

h: Rue de la Mission-Marchand is a short street of about 70 metres in the Auteuil district, between rue Pierre-Guérin and rue de la Source. Opened in 1900, it was named by decree of 3 January 1901 in memory of the crossing of Africa by the column of Commandant Jean-Baptiste Marchand, which reached Fashoda, on the Nile, in 1898; the French government had to order its withdrawal in the face of Kitchener's Anglo-Egyptian army, a crisis that preceded the rapprochement of the Entente Cordiale.

Crowley left rue Frochot in early July 1927. His correspondence bears the address 6 rue de la Mission-Marchand from 15 July to the end of November, and again in early December; on 26 December he was at the Hôtel Foyot. Jane Wolfe, discharged from the American Hospital, left for New York on 1 October.

His daughter Astarte Lulu Panthea, born on 26 November 1920 of his liaison with Ninette Shumway, came to see him on 26 October, then again on 26 November: that day, her seventh birthday, he took her to the circus. The timeline also mentions, under 10 November, a sex-magick operation with the American photographer Berenice Abbott, but it gives the same date and the same description for the year 1926, which leaves a doubt about the year and therefore about the place.

Two years later, in April 1929, when Crowley, refused a residence permit, left Paris for Brussels, Paris-Midi mentioned the bachelor flat he had allegedly long kept in Auteuil, in a quiet street, and interviewed one of his associates and some neighbours, who denied the rumours of black masses. The article does not name the street, and Crowley was then living on avenue de Suffren: the connection with rue de la Mission-Marchand remains a hypothesis.

The street, residential and quiet, has few numbers, from 1 to 8. The sources do not describe the building at No. 6, which can be seen from the pavement in this small part of Auteuil near rue de la Source.

h: The Foyot restaurant, at 33 rue de Tournon, facing the Palais du Luxembourg, took its name from Nicolas Foyot, a former cook to Louis-Philippe, who took it over after 1848. His successor Léopold Mourier, from 1891, created dishes there that became famous, as well as the so-called Foyot sauce. The hotel above it lodged Rilke, Santayana, T. S. Eliot and Dorothy Parker. On 4 April 1894 a bomb there seriously injured the poet Laurent Tailhade; the perpetrator was never identified. The restaurant closed in 1937 and the building was demolished shortly afterwards.

Crowley lodged at the Foyot, room 21, from 26 December 1927. Gerald Yorke, a young disciple and future financial backer, introduced himself at Le Bourget airport on 27 December, then came to see him at the hotel on the 31st; Crowley, for his part, placed their first meeting at the Foyot. On 5 March 1928 Kasimira Bass arrived, his new companion, whose presence soon provoked scenes with Ninette Shumway and Dorothea Walker. On 22 March the publisher Collins returned to him all rights to The Diary of a Drug Fiend. He stayed at the Foyot until May, before leaving for Cassis and Marseille.

Back in Paris, he settled two streets away, at the Hôtel Royal Condé, 10 rue de Condé, from 15 to 27 July 1928; Yorke, who was then providing him with a weekly allowance and setting up a publishing syndicate, joined him there. After a stay in the Alps, he returned there from 29 August to mid-September, then moved to 55 avenue de Suffren.

Nothing remains of the Foyot: at the corner of rue de Tournon and rue de Vaugirard there is now a small tree-planted space facing the Senate. On rue de Condé, the sources do not say what became of the Hôtel Royal Condé.

The Galignani family is of Italian origin: a Simone Galignani was already publishing a Latin grammar in Venice in 1520. Giovanni Antonio Galignani, from Brescia, taught languages in Paris, then opened an English bookshop in 1801. His sons John Anthony and William developed the business: a review of English literature, the daily Galignani's Messenger founded after 1814 for the English on the Continent, and cheap reprints of British authors until the 1852 copyright treaty. Their house on rue Vivienne, with a reading room and garden, served as a club for the English in Paris.

The bookshop moved under the arcades of rue de Rivoli in the mid-1850s (1855 or 1856 depending on the source) and claims the title of the first English bookshop established on the Continent. It is still run by descendants of the family; its wooden shelves date from the 1930s.

For Crowley, it was one of the places where he obtained his English reading matter. In September 1928 he moved to avenue de Suffren, and on 12 October, the day his new secretary Israel Regardie arrived from America, he bought at Galignani the Golden Verses of Pythagoras, two detective novels and a stamp. On 5 February 1929 he picked up recent mystery novels there, including Agatha Christie's Poirot Investigates and The Secret of Chimneys, as well as Raphael's astrological ephemeris for the year; on 2 March more detective novels, on 5 March Stevenson's The Dynamiter.

These purchases shortly preceded his forced departure: on 8 March 1929, his associates Maria de Miramar and Regardie were refused residence permits; Crowley, who was ill, obtained a delay, but Paris-Midi announced his expulsion on 16 April and he took the train to Brussels the following day.

The Librairie Galignani is still open at 224 rue de Rivoli, under the arcades. From the pavement one can recognise its shop window and sign, and one can go in: the English-language books are at the back of the shop.

À la Petite Chaise, at 36 rue de Grenelle, presents itself as one of the oldest restaurants in Paris. Its chroniclers date its origins to 1680, under Louis XIV, in an early 17th-century building on the old Grenelle road. Wine and meals were served there at the time; the name is said to come from an old word, chèze, meaning an isolated house. The owner of the house is said to have been Vincent Maynon, secretary to the king.

Tradition makes the place a meeting spot for the Regent Philippe d'Orléans and Cardinal Dubois in the 18th century, then for the Romantics in the 19th: Chateaubriand, George Sand, Musset, Juliette Récamier; later Toulouse-Lautrec, Édith Piaf and Juliette Gréco. These stories belong partly to the legend of the house, and the sources provide no proof of them.

In November 1928, Crowley was living at 55 avenue de Suffren. His private life was turbulent: Kasimira Bass, his companion since March, had left on 11 October taking 5,000 francs, had come back on the 23rd, then left him again on 3 November. Israel Regardie, who had arrived on 12 October, served as his secretary, and Gerald Yorke supported him financially.
It was in this context that he dined at the Petite Chaise on 12 November 1928 and afterwards recorded in his diary a kiss at 10:45 p.m. The person accompanying him is not identified.

The restaurant is still in business, lunch and dinner, serving traditional French cuisine. From the street one can see its old shopfront; the sign built into the entrance gate is said to date back to the origins of the house. The dining room retains floral wallpaper, chandeliers and wooden tables.

h: Avenue de Suffren, named after Admiral Pierre André de Suffren, was laid out around 1770, when the Champ-de-Mars was developed, between today's quai Branly and avenue de Lowendal. Transferred to the City of Paris in 1838, it was extended in 1867 to boulevard de Grenelle, now boulevard Garibaldi, at the cost of demolishing the Grenelle slaughterhouses. About 1,850 metres long, it separates the 7th and 15th arrondissements and runs along the south façade of the École Militaire. In Crowley's day, the Grande Roue built for the 1900 Exposition Universelle still stood at No. 74; it was not dismantled until 1937.

Crowley moved into No. 55 on Wednesday 19 September 1928; his letters to Gerald Yorke thereafter bear the letterhead “55 Avenue de Suffren, Paris VII”. The move was financed in part by the American Kasimira Bass, who had undertaken in writing to invest in his projects. On 11 October, while Crowley was playing at the chess club, she left the apartment taking 5,000 francs from his small safe; he filed a complaint the next day and found the money that same evening, hidden under a statue of Ho Tai. On that same 12 October, at 1:11 p.m., Israel Regardie arrived from America to become his secretary. Kasimira Bass returned on 23 October, then left for good on 3 November.

The following months were those of his meeting with Maria Teresa Ferrari de Miramar, born in Nicaragua in 1894, who would become his second wife; as early as 9 February 1929, Kasimira Bass allegedly threatened her on a bus, a sign that she was watching the building. Gerald Yorke came several times for the weekend, notably on 7 December 1928 and from 26 to 28 January 1929. The apartment was also the editorial workshop for Magick in Theory and Practice, printed by the Lecram Press: proofs of the prospectus on 17 January, choice of cover paper on 4 February, first page proofs around 14 or 15 February, and an advance copy of the first section on 12 April at 5:55 p.m.

It was here too that the inspectors of the foreigners' department arrived, from 17 January 1929, and that Crowley, bedridden, received his refusal of a residence permit on 8 March. Thanks to medical certificates, he stayed on until his departure for Brussels on 17 April 1929.

No. 55 avenue de Suffren is today a private residential building, not open to visitors; none of the sources reports a plaque. One can, however, walk along the avenue to the Champ-de-Mars and the site of the former Grande Roue, which Crowley could still see a few hundred metres from his home.

h: The Préfecture de Police occupies, on the Île de la Cité facing Notre-Dame, the former Caserne de la Cité, built from 1863 to 1867 to designs by Pierre-Victor Calliat to house the Paris Guard, on the site of the churches of Saint-Éloi and Saint-Germain-le-Vieux. When the Préfecture's former premises, near the Palais de Justice, were burned on 24 May 1871 at the end of the Commune, the administration moved into the barracks, at 7 boulevard du Palais. The Seine department bought the building at the end of 1878, and the Garde Républicaine shared it with the police until 1929, the very year of the Crowley affair.

Crowley, Regardie and Maria de Miramar came under the foreigners' department, responsible for the identity cards of foreign residents. On 17 January 1929, an inspector came to avenue de Suffren to enquire about these cards, about Crowley's drug use and about his travels over the past year; on 29 January, the head of the foreigners' office assured his friend Gerard Aumont that Crowley need not worry. Yet on 5 March a summons to the Préfecture was issued to the three residents. Being ill, Crowley obtained a postponement to Friday 8 March, when Regardie and Maria de Miramar went alone: they were handed refusals of residence dated 15 February, with orders to leave the country before 9 March. An inspector brought the same document to Crowley that afternoon.

Regardie called on the American consul, who replied that there were no personal charges against him: he was paying for his position as Crowley's secretary. Turned back to England on 10 March, Regardie and Maria de Miramar fell back on Brussels. Crowley, for his part, was allowed on 10 March to stay provisionally on account of his health, and kept himself there thanks to medical certificates. When the affair broke in the press in mid-April, the Préfecture confirmed the refusal of residence to British journalists while denying any link with the accusations of espionage; Crowley said he did not know the reason and demanded a public inquiry.

The building still houses the Préfecture de Police, renovated from 2009 to 2014. It is above all famous for the police uprising of 19 August 1944 and the German surrender signed on 25 August in the billiard room. Its façades can be seen from the parvis of Notre-Dame, boulevard du Palais or quai du Marché-Neuf; the offices are not open to the public.

h: The Gare du Nord replaced the Embarcadère de Belgique, opened in 1846 by Léonce Reynaud for the Creil line. Having become too small, this first building was dismantled and re-erected in Lille, where it forms the present Lille-Flandres station. The Compagnie des chemins de fer du Nord, chaired by James de Rothschild, commissioned a new station in 1857, whose design Jacques-Ignace Hittorff took over in 1861. Opened in 1864 and completed in 1865, it combines a train shed of cast iron, iron and glass some 200 metres long with a neoclassical façade of nearly 180 metres, crowned by 23 allegorical statues of cities, with the figure of Paris, by Pierre-Jules Cavelier, at the top.

It is the station for trains to Belgium, and it was here that Crowley's Parisian stay came to an end. After two days of uproar in the press, begun on 16 April 1929 by a Paris-Midi article accusing him of having served Germany during the war, Crowley spent the day of the 16th with reporters and photographers. The next morning, 17 April, he left for Brussels. According to Paris-Midi of 18 April, he took the 11:30 a.m. train at the Gare du Nord, closely watched by the Sûreté Générale, and told the journalist on the platform that he was leaving because he was forced to, but that he would return to learn the charges against him and to clear his name. He said he was going to Brussels to fetch his fiancée, Maria de Miramar, and his secretary Regardie, and accused his former associate Carl de Vidal Hunt of having fed the press.

The other sources differ on the details: the Crowley Timeline speaks of a 10 a.m. train, and the Manchester Guardian writes that he was escorted to the Franco-Belgian border. That same evening Crowley was registered at the Hôtel Métropole in Brussels, room 459. News of the “expulsion” went round the American and British newspapers.

The station is now a listed historic monument and ranks among the busiest in Europe. Hittorff's façade, its statues of cities and the great train shed remain visible from place Napoléon-III and rue de Dunkerque; the canopy added later in front of the façade hides part of the porticoes.

h: In the Middle Ages, the western tip of the Île de la Cité was made up of small separate islets, including the Île aux Juifs. It was there, on 18 March 1314, that Jacques de Molay, last Grand Master of the Order of the Temple, and Geoffroy de Charnay, preceptor of Normandy, were burned alive. That same day, on the parvis of Notre-Dame, the judges had sentenced them to life imprisonment for heresy; as the two men then proclaimed their innocence and denounced a conspiracy by Philip the Fair and Pope Clement V, they were deemed relapsed heretics and sent to the stake that very evening. The legend of a curse laid on the king and the pope has never been verified.

The islets were joined to the Île de la Cité during the construction of the Pont Neuf, completed in 1606. The land, later occupied by baths and then by a café-concert swept away by the flood of 1879, was bought by the City in 1884 and became the square du Vert-Galant, named after the nickname of Henri IV, whose equestrian statue, recast by Lemot in 1818, overlooks the site.

Thelema's link with Molay runs through the Gnostic Mass, Liber XV, written by Crowley in Moscow in 1913 for the O.T.O. and its Church, the Ecclesia Gnostica Catholica. In the Collect of the Saints, Molay appears under the Latin name Jacobus Burgundus Molensis, “the Martyr”, in all published versions. The O.T.O., whose name translates as Order of the Templars of the East, placed itself symbolically in the Templar line; Crowley took in it the name Baphomet, the idol that the trials of 1307-1314 attributed to the Templars. The eleventh collect, “The End”, is a prayer for those whose life has ended, that they may accomplish their true will.

A plaque commemorating the execution of 1314 is placed on the site of the former islet, at the entrance to the square, below the Pont Neuf and the statue of Henri IV. The square, of about 1,640 square metres, planted with willows, horse chestnuts and a ginkgo, is sometimes submerged when the Seine floods. Every 18 March, the map suggests reading the eleventh collect there and laying flowers.

h: Alphonse-Louis Constant was born in Paris on 8 February 1810, at 5 rue des Fossés-Saint-Germain-des-Prés (now rue de l'Ancienne-Comédie), the son of a shoemaker. A seminarian at Saint-Sulpice, he renounced the priesthood in 1836 after the diaconate, moved in socialist circles, became close to Flora Tristan and was imprisoned for his writings. Around 1851, under the name Éliphas Lévi, he turned to occultism: Dogme et rituel de la haute magie (1854-1856), Histoire de la magie and La Clef des grands mystères (1861) made him a reference for French esotericism, and then for the Golden Dawn.

In May 1864 he settled at 155 rue de Sèvres, where he spent his last years, suffering from a heart condition contracted during the siege of 1870, then from severe bronchitis in 1874. He died there on 31 May 1875, at around two in the afternoon, aged 65. His religious funeral took place at Saint-François-Xavier; he was buried in the Ivry cemetery under a simple wooden cross, but his remains were exhumed in 1881 and placed in the common grave.

Crowley, born in October 1875, a few months after his death, believed himself to be the reincarnation of Lévi, a conviction encouraged by this coincidence of dates. He owed him a great deal: at the end of 1913 The Equinox published the English translation of La Clef des grands mystères, which takes up nearly half the volume, and Crowley adopted the name Baphomet, a figure Lévi had popularised through his famous drawing in Dogme et rituel. Lévi also appears among the saints of the Gnostic Mass, under his civil name Alphonse Louis Constant.

No. 155 now lies alongside the site of the Hôpital Necker-Enfants malades, whose main address is 149 rue de Sèvres. This complex combines the hospital founded in 1778 by Suzanne Necker, where Laennec invented the stethoscope in 1816, and the first paediatric hospital in the Western world, opened in 1802; the two institutions merged in 1920. Nothing marks Lévi on site, and his grave at Ivry no longer exists. Every 31 May, the map suggests a gathering, the eleventh collect and a laying of flowers.

h: The enclos du Temple was the seat of the Templars for the province of France and their largest commandery in the kingdom. Its exact founding date remains uncertain: a first house, the Vieux Temple, existed around 1140 near the place de Grève, and a charter of 1146 mentions a house of the Temple in Paris. The fortified estate covered about six hectares of today's Marais, around a great tower, a church and a palace.

At dawn on Friday 13 October 1307, on the secret orders of Philip the Fair, the Templars were arrested throughout the kingdom. Jacques de Molay and some 140 brothers of the Paris house were seized in the enclos; some were killed, the others imprisoned. The order was dissolved in 1312 and its property passed to the Hospitallers, who made the enclos the Grand Priory of the Temple. The great tower served as a prison for the royal family from 13 August 1792: Louis XVI left it on 21 January 1793 for the scaffold, and Louis XVII died there in 1795. Napoleon had it razed from 1808; the church and cloister had disappeared in 1796, and the Grand Prior's palace fell in 1853.

For Thelema, the Temple refers to the Templar lineage symbolically claimed by the O.T.O., the Order of the Templars of the East, which Crowley joined in 1910 and of which he became head in 1925, having proclaimed himself such as early as 1921. In it he bore the name Baphomet, taken from the accusations levelled against the Templars during the trials opened by the arrests of 1307, and he included their last Grand Master among the saints of the Gnostic Mass. No source indicates any particular visit by Crowley to this site.

Almost nothing remains of the enclos. The square du Temple, designed by Adolphe Alphand and inaugurated on 11 November 1857, partly covers the site of the great tower; since 2017 it has been called square du Temple – Elie-Wiesel and contains a bandstand of 1900 and a memorial stele to the deported children of the 3rd arrondissement. Blue markings on the ground, on rue Eugène-Spuller, outline the turrets and the tower, and a plaque at the corner of rue Dupetit-Thouars and rue Gabriel-Vicaire superimposes the plan of the enclos on today's streets. Every 13 October, the map suggests a gathering, a reading and a laying of flowers.

h: Opened in 1804 and named after Louis XIV's confessor, Père-Lachaise is the largest green space in Paris. Gérard Encausse rests there. Born on 13 July 1865 in A Coruña, to a French chemist father and a Spanish mother, he grew up in Paris, became a doctor of medicine there in 1894 and took the name Papus, a genius of medicine in the Nuctemeron of Apollonius of Tyana, which Lévi had translated as an appendix to his Dogme et rituel.

A prolific author, notably of Le Tarot des Bohémiens (1889) and Traité méthodique de science occulte (1891), he founded the review L'Initiation, created the Martinist Order in 1891 with Augustin Chaboseau, co-directed the Kabbalistic Order of the Rose-Cross and in 1893 received the episcopate of Jules Doinel's Gnostic Church. He travelled to Russia in 1901, 1905 and 1906 to see Nicholas II. A military doctor during the Great War, he contracted tuberculosis and died in Paris on 25 October 1916, aged 51.

Papus is a link in the history that Crowley inherited. On 24 June 1908, at an international Masonic conference he organised in Paris, he received from Theodor Reuss a charter for the Rite of Memphis-Misraïm in France, and probably also the Xth degree of the O.T.O. for France; he then helped Reuss create the Gnostic Catholic Church attached to the O.T.O. Reuss and his associates held from him the right to work the Martinist rites. Crowley, admitted by Reuss in 1910, included “Docteur Gérard Encausse” among the saints of the Gnostic Mass. The sources document no personal meeting between the two men.

According to the association Amis et passionnés du Père-Lachaise, the grave is in the 93rd division, avenue Greffülhe. Two plaques appear on it: one presents him as physician, philosopher, writer and Grand Master of the Martinist Order, with a date of death engraved as 23 October 1916; the other bears a thought by Papus on prayer. His son, Dr Philippe Encausse (1906-1984), is also named there. Every 25 October, the map suggests a gathering at the grave, the reading of the eleventh collect of Liber XV and a laying of flowers.
